new_statements.quote: Unlike languages like English and Mandarin Chinese, Maonan does not assign suprasegmental features to different syllables to differentiate compound words, word compound or phrases. For example, in Mandarin, the compound word dōngxi with the second syllable unaccented, means ‘thing’, but the word compound dōngxi, with both syllables stressed, means ‘east and west’ [...]. In Maonan, ˀda¹ɬaːn¹ (eye-red), with both syllables stressed, means either ‘jealous’ or ‘the eyes become red’. // p. 105: Maonan is a tonal language which distinguishes words by ‘tonemes’. Such use of suprasegmental features plays a significant role in Maonan lexicology.
new_statements.citation: Lu, Tian Qiao. 2008. A Grammar of Maonan. Boca Raton, FL: Universal Publishers.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Maonan is a tone language (8 tones plus a borrowed low-falling tone); the grammar contains no rule locating word stress. Its one statement on stress says that, unlike English or Mandarin, Maonan does not use differential stress (or other suprasegmental features) across the syllables of a word to distinguish compounds from phrases: in a disyllabic compound such as ˀda¹ɬaːn¹ 'eye-red' = 'jealous'/'eyes become red' both syllables are stressed (i.e. no unstressed/neutral-tone syllable, no culminative word stress). Stress is thus non-contrastive and effectively absent as a word-level parameter; tone and tone sandhi carry the lexical and morphological load (suprafixation).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Tone-related: tone sandhi occurs in the first or second syllable of compounds depending on the closeness of binding (pp. 104-105, Table 37), never in the final syllable; clause-final particles have 'weakened', unstable tones (p. 289); grammaticalised words are 'reduced in prominence' (ch. 7).
new_statements.domain_note: The statement concerns disyllabic compound words vs. phrases (word level). The passage was reconstructed from overlapping scanned highlight snippets returned by the Open Library search-inside API, not from a full page image; scanned normalisations: 'déngxi' -> dōngxi, '"da'/a:n’' -> ˀda¹ɬaːn¹ (tone superscripts not legible in scanned). The elided '[...]' portion is the parallel English blackbird/black bird example.
new_statements.identity_note: Lu 2008 describes the Maonan of Huanjiang Maonan Autonomous County, Guangxi (author's native variety; Xianan/Huanjiang dialect area) — same languoid as maon1241; no dialect split needed. Coyaud 1987 and maonan.org describe the same standard variety (based on Liang Min 1980).

sources.note: Initials (incl. prenasalised), finals, six tones in open syllables (42, 231, 51, 24, 44, 213) and long/short checked-syllable tones; nothing on stress/accent.
